TikTok engagement rate is the share of a creator's audience that interacts with their content, and it is one of the fastest ways to sanity-check a creator before you partner. As a rough guide, smaller creators post higher engagement rates than large ones, and anything visibly below the norm for a creator's size is a flag. But for TikTok Shop, engagement is a filter, not the goal. Sales are the goal.

How to calculate it

The common formula:

Engagement rate = (likes + comments + shares) ÷ views × 100

Some use follower count as the denominator instead of views. Views-based is more honest on TikTok, where content reaches well beyond followers. Pick one method and apply it consistently when comparing creators.

Rough benchmarks by size

Engagement generally falls as audience grows, because bigger audiences are less tightly connected:

  • Nano and micro creators tend to post the highest rates and often the best conversion for TikTok Shop.
  • Mid-tier creators sit lower but still healthy.
  • Large creators show the lowest rates, offset by raw reach.

Treat specific percentages as directional and always compare a creator against others of similar size, not against a single universal number.

Why engagement matters less than you think for Shop

Here is the part most guides miss: for TikTok Shop, engagement rate is a vetting signal, not the outcome. A creator with modest engagement who consistently sells your category beats a high-engagement creator who has never moved a product. Category selling history is a stronger predictor of GMV than engagement rate.

Consistency is the variable that actually compounds. One seller described the curve in a r/TikTokshop thread: "I joined 3 months ago and went from selling 500 per show to 1000 per show to 2000, and now I'm selling upwards of 5000 to 6000 per show, six days a week" (r/TikTokshop). No engagement-rate benchmark predicts that. Showing up six days a week did.

So use engagement to catch problems, not to pick winners.

What engagement catches

  • Fake followers. High follower count with low engagement suggests bought audience. See vetting creators.
  • Dead audiences. A creator whose viewers do not interact will not drive action.
  • Comment quality. Read the comments, not just the count. Questions and buying intent beat a wall of emojis.

How to use it in practice

  1. Filter your shortlist for category selling first.
  2. Use engagement to flag anyone whose numbers look bought or inflated.
  3. Read comments on finalists for real buying intent.
  4. Compare like-for-like by creator size.

The takeaway

Engagement rate is a cheap, fast filter that catches fake and dead audiences, and a weak way to pick sellers. For TikTok Shop, weight selling history above engagement, and use engagement to avoid mistakes rather than to chase a number.

Want creators pre-vetted on the signals that predict sales? Book a call, or search proven sellers in your niche.
